In [[geometry]], an '''incidence''' [[Relation (mathematics)|relation]] is a [[heterogeneous relation]] that captures the idea being expressed when phrases such as "a point ''lies on'' a line" or "a line is ''contained in'' a plane" are used. The most basic incidence relation is that between a point, {{math|''P''}}, and a line, {{math|''l''}}, sometimes denoted {{math|''P'' I ''l''}}. If {{math|''P''}} and {{math|''l''}} are incident, {{math|''P'' I ''l''}}, the pair {{math|(''P'', ''l'')}} is called a ''flag''.

There are many expressions used in common language to describe incidence (for example, a line ''passes through'' a point, a point ''lies in'' a plane, etc.) but the term "incidence" is preferred because it does not have the additional connotations that these other terms have, and it can be used in a symmetric manner. Statements such as "line {{math|''l''<sub>1</sub>}} intersects line {{math|''l''<sub>2</sub>}}" are also statements about incidence relations, but in this case, it is because this is a shorthand way of saying that "there exists a point {{math|''P''}} that is incident with both line {{math|''l''<sub>1</sub>}} and line {{math|''l''<sub>2</sub>}}". When one type of object can be thought of as a set of the other type of object (''viz''., a plane is a set of points) then an incidence relation may be viewed as [[subset|containment]].

Statements such as "any two lines in a plane meet" are called ''incidence propositions''. This particular statement is true in a [[projective plane]], though not true in the [[Euclidean plane]] where lines may be [[Parallel (geometry)|parallel]]. Historically, [[projective geometry]] was developed in order to make the propositions of incidence true without exceptions, such as those caused by the existence of parallels. From the point of view of [[synthetic geometry]],  projective geometry ''should be'' developed using such propositions as [[axiom]]s. This is most significant for projective planes due to the universal validity of [[Desargues' theorem]] in higher dimensions.

In contrast, the [[analytic geometry|analytic approach]] is to define [[projective space]] based on [[linear algebra]] and utilizing [[homogeneous co-ordinates]]. The propositions of incidence are derived from the following basic result on [[vector space]]s: given subspaces {{math|''U''}} and {{math|''W''}} of a (finite-dimensional) vector space {{math|''V''}}, the dimension of their intersection is  {{math|dim ''U'' + dim ''W'' &minus; dim (''U'' + ''W'')}}. Bearing in mind that the geometric dimension of the projective space {{math|'''P'''(''V'')}} associated to {{math|''V''}} is {{math|dim ''V'' &minus; 1}} and that the geometric dimension of any subspace is positive, the basic proposition of incidence in this setting can take the form: [[linear subspace]]s {{math|''L''}} and {{math|''M''}} of projective space {{math|''P''}} meet provided {{math|dim ''L'' + dim ''M'' ≥ dim ''P''}}.<ref>Joel G. Broida & S. Gill Williamson (1998) ''A Comprehensive Introduction to Linear Algebra'', Theorem 2.11, p 86, [[Addison-Wesley]] {{ISBN|0-201-50065-5}}. The theorem says that {{math|1=dim (''L'' + ''M'') = dim ''L'' + dim ''M'' &minus; dim (''L'' ∩ ''M'')}}. Thus {{math|dim ''L'' + dim ''M'' > dim ''P''}} implies {{math|dim (''L'' ∩ ''M'') > 0}}.</ref>

The following sections are limited to [[projective plane]]s defined over [[field (mathematics)|fields]], often denoted by {{math|PG(2, ''F'')}}, where {{math|''F''}} is a field, or {{math|'''P'''<sup>2</sup>''F''}}. However these computations can be naturally extended to higher-dimensional projective spaces, and the field may be replaced by a [[division ring]] (or skewfield) provided that one pays attention to the fact that multiplication is not [[Commutative property|commutative]] in that case.

=={{math|PG(2,''F'')}}==
{{main|Homogeneous coordinates}}

Let {{math|''V''}} be the three-dimensional vector space defined over the field {{math|''F''}}. The projective plane {{math|1='''P'''(''V'') = PG(2, ''F'')}} consists of the one-dimensional vector subspaces of {{math|''V''}}, called ''points'', and the two-dimensional vector subspaces of {{math|''V''}}, called ''lines''. Incidence of a point and a line is given by containment of the one-dimensional subspace in the two-dimensional subspace.

Fix a basis for {{math|''V''}} so that we may describe its vectors as coordinate triples (with respect to that basis). A one-dimensional vector subspace consists of a non-zero vector and all of its scalar multiples. The non-zero scalar multiples, written as coordinate triples, are the homogeneous coordinates of the given point, called ''point coordinates''. With respect to this basis, the solution space of a single linear equation {{math|1={(''x'', ''y'', ''z'') {{!}} ''ax'' + ''by'' + ''cz'' = 0}}} is a two-dimensional subspace of {{math|''V''}}, and hence a line of {{math|'''P'''(''V'')}}. This line may be denoted by ''line coordinates'' {{math|[''a'', ''b'', ''c'']}}, which are also homogeneous coordinates since non-zero scalar multiples would give the same line. Other notations are also widely used. Point coordinates may be written as column vectors, {{math|(''x'', ''y'', ''z'')}}<sup>T</sup>, with colons, {{math|(''x'' : ''y'' : ''z'')}}, or with a subscript, {{math|(''x'', ''y'', ''z'')<sub>P</sub>}}. Correspondingly, line coordinates may be written as row vectors, {{math|(''a'', ''b'', ''c'')}}, with colons, {{math|[''a'' : ''b'' : ''c'']}} or with a subscript, {{math|(''a'', ''b'', ''c'')<sub>L</sub>}}. Other variations are also possible.

==Incidence expressed algebraically==

Given a point {{math|1=''P'' = (''x'', ''y'', ''z'')}} and a line {{math|1=''l'' = [''a'', ''b'', ''c'']}}, written in terms of point and line coordinates, the point is incident with the line (often written as {{math|''P'' I ''l''}}), if and only if,

:: {{math|1=''ax'' + ''by'' + ''cz'' = 0}}.

This can be expressed in other notations as:
:<math>ax + by + cz = [a,b,c] \cdot (x,y,z) =(a,b,c)_L \cdot (x,y,z)_P =</math>

:<math> = [a:b:c] \cdot (x:y:z) = (a,b,c) \left ( \begin{matrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{matrix} \right ) = 0. </math>

No matter what notation is employed, when the homogeneous coordinates of the point and line are just considered as ordered triples, their incidence is expressed as having their [[dot product]] equal 0.

==The line incident with a pair of distinct points==
Let {{math|''P''<sub>1</sub>}} and {{math|''P''<sub>2</sub>}} be a pair of distinct points with homogeneous coordinates {{math|(''x''<sub>1</sub>, ''y''<sub>1</sub>, ''z''<sub>1</sub>)}} and {{math|(''x''<sub>2</sub>, ''y''<sub>2</sub>, ''z''<sub>2</sub>)}} respectively. These points determine a unique line {{math|''l''}} with an equation of the form {{math|1=''ax'' + ''by'' + ''cz'' = 0}} and must satisfy the equations:
: {{math|1=''ax''<sub>1</sub> + ''by''<sub>1</sub> + ''cz''<sub>1</sub> = 0}} and
: {{math|1=''ax''<sub>2</sub> + ''by''<sub>2</sub> + ''cz''<sub>2</sub> = 0}}. 
In matrix form this system of simultaneous linear equations can be expressed as:
:<math>\left( \begin{matrix} x & y & z \\ x_1 & y_1 & z_1 \\ x_2 & y_2 & z_2 \end{matrix} \right) \left( \begin{matrix} a \\ b \\ c \end{matrix} \right) = \left( \begin{matrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{matrix} \right).</math>
This system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the [[determinant]],
:<math> \left| \begin{matrix} x & y & z \\ x_1 & y_1 & z_1 \\x_2 & y_2 & z_2 \end{matrix} \right| = 0.</math> 
Expansion of this determinantal equation produces a homogeneous linear equation, which must be the equation of line {{math|''l''}}. Therefore, up to a common non-zero constant factor we have {{math|1=''l'' = [''a'', ''b'', ''c'']}} where:
: {{math|1=''a'' = ''y''<sub>1</sub>''z''<sub>2</sub> - ''y''<sub>2</sub>''z''<sub>1</sub>}},
: {{math|1=''b'' = ''x''<sub>2</sub>''z''<sub>1</sub> - ''x''<sub>1</sub>''z''<sub>2</sub>}}, and
: {{math|1=''c'' = ''x''<sub>1</sub>''y''<sub>2</sub> - ''x''<sub>2</sub>''y''<sub>1</sub>}}.

In terms of the [[Triple product|scalar triple product]] notation for vectors, the equation of this line may be written as:
: {{math|1=''P'' ⋅ ''P''<sub>1</sub> × ''P''<sub>2</sub> = 0}},
where {{math|1=''P'' = (''x'', ''y'', ''z'')}} is a generic point.

===Collinearity===
{{main|Collinear}}

Points that are incident with the same line are said to be ''collinear''. The set of all points incident with the same line is called a [[Projective range|range]].

If {{math|1=''P''<sub>1</sub> = (''x''<sub>1</sub>, ''y''<sub>1</sub>, ''z''<sub>1</sub>), ''P''<sub>2</sub> = (''x''<sub>2</sub>, ''y''<sub>2</sub>, ''z''<sub>2</sub>)}}, and {{math|1=''P''<sub>3</sub> = (''x''<sub>3</sub>, ''y''<sub>3</sub>, ''z''<sub>3</sub>)}}, then these points are collinear if and only if
:<math> \left| \begin{matrix} x_1 & y_1 & z_1 \\ x_2 & y_2 & z_2 \\ x_3 & y_3 & z_3 \end{matrix} \right| = 0,</math>
i.e., if and only if the [[determinant]] of the homogeneous coordinates of the points is equal to zero.

For more than 3 points this can be generalized as a rank test: <math>P_1, ..., P_n</math> with the homogenous coordinates <math>(x_1, y_1, z_1), ..., (x_n, y_n, z_n)</math> are collinear if and only if<blockquote><math>\operatorname{rank}

\begin{pmatrix}
x_1 & y_1 & z_1 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\
x_n & y_n & z_n
\end{pmatrix}

< 3</math>.</blockquote>According to the [[Gram matrix|Gram determinant test]], whether the matrix <math>P</math> above has less than full rank is equivalent to <math>\det(P^{\mathsf{T}} P) = 0</math>.

==Intersection of a pair of lines==
{{main|Line-line intersection}}
Let {{math|1=''l''<sub>1</sub> = [''a''<sub>1</sub>, ''b''<sub>1</sub>, ''c''<sub>1</sub>]}} and {{math|1=''l''<sub>2</sub> = [''a''<sub>2</sub>, ''b''<sub>2</sub>, ''c''<sub>2</sub>]}} be a pair of distinct lines.  Then the intersection of lines {{math|''l''<sub>1</sub>}} and {{math|''l''<sub>2</sub>}} is point a {{math|1=''P'' = (''x''<sub>0</sub>, ''y''<sub>0</sub>, ''z''<sub>0</sub>)}} that is the simultaneous solution (up to a scalar factor) of the system of linear equations:
: {{math|1=''a''<sub>1</sub>''x'' + ''b''<sub>1</sub>''y'' + ''c''<sub>1</sub>''z'' = 0}} and
: {{math|1=''a''<sub>2</sub>''x'' + ''b''<sub>2</sub>''y'' + ''c''<sub>2</sub>''z'' = 0}}.
The solution of this system gives:
: {{math|1=''x''<sub>0</sub> = ''b''<sub>1</sub>''c''<sub>2</sub> - ''b''<sub>2</sub>''c''<sub>1</sub>}},
: {{math|1=''y''<sub>0</sub> = ''a''<sub>2</sub>''c''<sub>1</sub> - ''a''<sub>1</sub>''c''<sub>2</sub>}}, and
: {{math|1=''z''<sub>0</sub> = ''a''<sub>1</sub>''b''<sub>2</sub> - ''a''<sub>2</sub>''b''<sub>1</sub>}}.

Alternatively, consider another line {{math|1=''l'' = [''a'', ''b'', ''c'']}} passing through the point {{math|''P''}}, that is, the homogeneous coordinates of {{math|''P''}} satisfy the equation:
:{{math|1=''ax''+ ''by'' + ''cz'' = 0}}.  
Combining this equation with the two that define {{math|''P''}}, we can seek a non-trivial solution of the matrix equation:
:<math>\left( \begin{matrix} a & b & c \\ a_1 & b_1 & c_1 \\ a_2 & b_2 & c_2 \end{matrix} \right) \left( \begin{matrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{matrix} \right) = \left( \begin{matrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{matrix} \right).</math>
Such a solution exists provided the determinant,
:<math> \left| \begin{matrix} a & b & c \\ a_1 & b_1 & c_1 \\a_2 & b_2 & c_2 \end{matrix} \right| = 0.</math> 
The coefficients of {{math|''a'', ''b''}} and {{math|''c''}} in this equation give the homogeneous coordinates of {{math|''P''}}.

The equation of the generic line passing through the point {{math|''P''}} in scalar triple product notation is:
: {{math|1=''l'' ⋅ ''l''<sub>1</sub> × ''l''<sub>2</sub> = 0}}.

===Concurrence===
Lines that meet at the same point are said to be [[concurrent lines|''concurrent'']]. The set of all lines in a plane incident with the same point is called a ''pencil of lines'' centered at that point. The computation of the intersection of two lines shows that the entire pencil of lines centered at a point is determined by any two of the lines that intersect at that point. It immediately follows that the algebraic condition for three lines, {{math|[''a''<sub>1</sub>, ''b''<sub>1</sub>,  ''c''<sub>1</sub>], [''a''<sub>2</sub>, ''b''<sub>2</sub>, ''c''<sub>2</sub>], [''a''<sub>3</sub>, ''b''<sub>3</sub>, ''c''<sub>3</sub>]}} to be concurrent is that the determinant,
:<math> \left| \begin{matrix} a_1 & b_1 & c_1 \\a_2 & b_2 & c_2 \\ a_3 & b_3 & c_3 \end{matrix} \right| = 0.</math>
